opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been one of the most surprising parts of this whole journey, honestly. When we started building these models, the mental picture was pretty narrow: a designer or an artist wants a specific image, they describe it, they get it. And that use case is absolutely real. But once you put a capable model in front of millions of people, they find all sorts of things you never planned for.

On the playful side, a lot of it is just people having fun with themselves and their friends. They'll take a photo of their dog and put it in a Renaissance painting, or reimagine their living room as a spaceship, or make a silly birthday card that's full of inside jokes. There's something really delightful about that. It's less about producing a polished asset and more about play, a kind of visual conversation. And I think that's a legitimate and valuable use. It's not frivolous. Creativity for its own sake matters to people.

What's been more interesting to me, and I didn't fully anticipate it, is the information-seeking side. People increasingly use image generation and editing to understand something or think through an idea. Someone wants to see what a haircut might look like before they commit. Someone wants a diagram that explains how a process works. Someone is planning a garden and wants to visualize it in different seasons. Or a teacher wants an illustration of a historical scene for a lesson. In those cases the image isn't really the end product. It's a way of communicating or reasoning visually.

That shift has big implications for how we build and evaluate these models. If people are using images to learn or make decisions, then things like accuracy, consistency, and correctly rendering text and structure become much more important than pure aesthetic quality. A beautiful diagram that's subtly wrong is actually worse than a plain one that's right. So we've had to think harder about grounding, about the model understanding the world and not just producing something that looks plausible.

It also blurs the line between image generation and the broader assistant experience. When the model can reason about what you're asking, ask clarifying questions, and iterate with you, it starts to feel less like a tool you prompt and more like a collaborator you think alongside. I find that exciting. It suggests images are becoming another native way for people to communicate with these systems, alongside text, rather than a separate specialized feature.

So overall I'm pretty optimistic. The breadth of uses tells us people find real value here. Our job is to make sure the model is good enough, and responsible enough, to support both the fun stuff and the stuff where getting it right actually matters.

fable-5.1.text:
It's honestly one of the most fun parts of working on this stuff, because the range is so much wider than what we imagined when we were building it. On the playful side, people take a photo of their dog and ask for it in a Renaissance portrait, or they put themselves into a movie poster, or they just type something absurd to see what comes out. And I think that's great. That kind of play is how people develop intuition for what the model is, what it's good at, where it falls apart. It's not frivolous. It's how you learn the tool.

But what surprised me more is the information-seeking side. People are using image generation to understand things, not just to make pretty pictures. Someone wants to see what a specific knot looks like from a different angle, or how a room might look with the furniture rearranged, or what a historical artifact might have looked like intact. It becomes a kind of visual reasoning aid. A sketchpad for ideas you can't easily put into words.

And that second category raises the bar for us in an interesting way. When someone is playing, a weird hand or a wrong detail is funny. When someone is trying to learn something, that same error is misinformation, and they may not know enough to catch it. So we think a lot about that tension. The same model, the same prompt box, and the stakes are completely different depending on intent.

What I try to resist is drawing a hard line between the two. A lot of the playful uses are secretly informational. A kid asking for a volcano cross-section with a dragon inside it is still learning what a volcano looks like. And a lot of serious uses have a playful quality, like an architect trying twenty ridiculous facade variations just to loosen up their thinking. I think the healthiest way to view it is that these models are becoming a general visual interface, and people will use that interface for exactly as many purposes as they've always used images for, which is nearly everything.

astra-6.text:
I think that range is part of what makes these models interesting. Sometimes you have a very specific thing in mind, and you’re trying to get the model to help you visualize it. Other times, you’re just playing—you try something, see what comes back, and that gives you another idea. The surprise is part of the value.

And I don’t think those are completely separate activities. Playing can be a way of exploring a question or figuring out what you actually want. But when you move toward seeking information, the expectations change. An image can look very convincing without being accurate. So there’s a distinction between using a model to imagine what something could look like and using it to understand what something really looks like. Both are interesting uses, but you need to know which one you’re doing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a really interesting spectrum. Sometimes people just want to play—to see what happens when they combine a couple of ideas or imagine something that doesn’t exist. That’s a valuable use in itself. It gives people a way to explore and express things that might otherwise be difficult to communicate.

And then there are uses where people are looking for information: what does this object look like, or how might something work? There, the expectations are different. A model can generate an image that looks very convincing without being accurate. So I think the interesting question is how we help people understand when they’re using a tool for imagination and when they can actually rely on it to learn something about the world.
